snapshots.name: Verus
snapshots.body: Marcus's grandfather, the first figure credited in the book's opening catalogue of formative influences. From him Marcus says he learned gentleness and freedom from anger.

snapshots.name: Diognetus
snapshots.body: An early teacher credited with steering the young Marcus away from trivial pursuits and superstition. His influence appears early in the catalogue of debts that opens the book.

snapshots.name: Rusticus
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher credited with turning Marcus toward serious philosophical study and away from mere rhetorical display. Marcus says it was Rusticus who first lent him the writings of Epictetus.

snapshots.name: Apollonius
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher credited with instilling in Marcus a sense of genuine independence and steadiness of purpose. His example shows Marcus what firmness without harshness looks like.

snapshots.name: Sextus
snapshots.body: A philosopher credited with teaching Marcus mildness and the model of a household governed by natural affection rather than force. His example of unaffected seriousness leaves a lasting impression.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Grammarian
snapshots.body: A teacher of grammar and rhetoric credited with teaching Marcus not to correct others' faults of speech harshly. He is distinguished in the text from another teacher of the same name, a Platonist philosopher.

snapshots.name: Fronto
snapshots.body: A rhetorician who taught Marcus to recognize the envy, deceit, and hypocrisy that can accompany absolute power. His observations on tyranny inform Marcus's own wariness as emperor.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Platonic
snapshots.body: A Platonist philosopher credited with teaching Marcus not to plead pressure of business as an excuse for neglecting friends. He is distinguished in the text from the grammarian of the same name.

snapshots.name: Catulus
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with showing Marcus not to dismiss a friend's complaint, even an unjust one, without trying to set things right. His example models a generosity Marcus clearly admired.

snapshots.name: Severus
snapshots.body: Marcus's brother, credited with introducing him to the idea of a community governed by equal law and equal speech for all. Through him Marcus says he came to admire Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, and Brutus.

snapshots.name: Claudius Maximus
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher credited with modeling self-command and cheerfulness even in illness. Marcus recalls him as a man whose character matched his teaching without any need for display.

snapshots.name: Antoninus
snapshots.body: Marcus's adoptive father and predecessor as emperor, held up repeatedly through the book as a model of steady, unshowy virtue in public life. Marcus returns again and again to his example of mildness, patience, and devotion to duty.

snapshots.name: Epictetus
snapshots.body: A Stoic philosopher, once a slave, whose recorded teachings Marcus quotes and returns to throughout the book. His sayings on what is and is not within a person's control run through much of Marcus's own thinking.

snapshots.name: Chrysippus
snapshots.body: An early Stoic philosopher whose systematic writings underlie much of the school's logic and physics. Marcus cites him briefly among the philosophers whose arguments he weighs against the fact of death.

snapshots.name: Theophrastus
snapshots.body: A philosopher, successor to Aristotle, cited by Marcus for a distinction between sins committed in passion and those committed in cold calculation. Marcus takes up the comparison to reflect on which kind is worse.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose ideal cities and forms Marcus invokes more than once, usually to set against the plainer demands of his own daily duty. He is treated as an authority worth citing, not a rival system to refute.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The philosopher held up throughout as an example of calm reasoning and indifference to popular opinion. Marcus returns to him as a model of how to face both petty annoyance and mortal danger.

snapshots.name: ruling part
snapshots.body: Marcus's term for the governing faculty of the mind, the part of a person capable of judgment and choice regardless of outward circumstance. He returns to it again and again as the one thing genuinely within a person's own power.
